entities.name: Natural History Museum, Vienna
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Natural History Museum Vienna (Naturhistorisches Museum Wien), opened in 1889 in Gottfried Semper's twin-towered Renaissance palace on Maria-Theresien-Platz, is one of the world's oldest and most scientifically significant natural history museums — holding 30 million objects including the Venus of Willendorf (24,000 BCE), the Hallstatt-Dachstein archaeological collection defining European Iron Age cultures, and one of the world's five largest meteorite collections. The museum's Habsburg imperial collections represent the cumulative scientific acquisitions of Europe's most acquisitive dynasty.

The Habsburgs began assembling natural history specimens in the 16th century under Rudolf II, who employed alchemists, astronomers, and naturalists at his Prague court. Maria Theresia organized the imperial collections and established the court Naturalienkabinett in 1748. The collections expanded through the voyages of the Novara (1857-1859), Austria's only circumnavigation expedition, and 400 years of imperial acquisitions from around the world.

The Venus of Willendorf — an 11 cm limestone figurine of a female form, carved approximately 25,000 BCE, discovered near Willendorf, Austria in 1908 — is one of the oldest known works of representational art and the most celebrated prehistoric sculpture in the world. Its exaggerated female features have made it central to feminist art history and human evolutionary debates. The museum's meteorite collection includes specimens from the Moon and Mars, and a fragment of the Tissint meteorite (the most recently fallen Martian meteorite) collected in 2011.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Natural History Museum Vienna's Venus of Willendorf — a 25,000-year-old figurine discovered in 1908 — became the most celebrated prehistoric art object in the world, transforming understanding of Paleolithic human creativity and sexual symbolism.
